results.note: The Table 4 definition, inclusion of never-cannabis users, six country percentages, South African cannabis prevalence and cross-country median are supported. Tables 2/4 display n = 16/13 for Japan and 8/7 for Nigeria, respectively. However, this supplied text does not explicitly define these n entries as unweighted observed counts. Table 4 calls its estimates projected; Table 2 footnote 6 specifies projected cumulative estimates for respondents younger than 29, and Methods 2.1/2.3 describe survey weighting and cumulative estimation. Therefore I can confirm the displayed n entries, but cannot certify the added raw/unweighted label or attribute the entire discrepancy solely to weighting. This is an unresolved count-definition issue, not evidence that n is weighted. Independently, 13/16 = 81.25% and 7/8 = 87.5%, unlike the reported 83.2% and 77.8%. The descriptive/causal qualification is supported by 4.1.
results.corrected_extracted: Table 4 estimates the percentage of people using other illicit drugs by age 29 who had not already used cannabis when other-drug use began; this includes people who never used cannabis, not just those who later used it. The country-specific weighted cumulative estimates in its Total column are USA 11.4%, New Zealand 12.7%, Japan 83.2% and Nigeria 77.8%. The corresponding displayed n entries for other-drug use in Table 2 and not-already-cannabis histories in Table 4 are 16/13 in Japan and 8/7 in Nigeria. The supplied text does not explicitly define these n entries as unweighted observed counts; Table 4 labels its estimates projected, and Table 2 also notes projection for younger respondents. The reported percentages should therefore not be reconstructed as simple fractions of the displayed n entries. South Africa has 59.2% and Mexico 48.4%; the authors describe South Africa’s cannabis prevalence of 8.5% as moderate relative to the cross-country median of 9.8%. Thus not-cannabis-first histories also occur where cannabis use is moderate. Correspondence across countries is descriptive and does not establish prevalence as a cause of initiation order; the limitations warn that prevalence does not necessarily map to supply, demand or attitudes.
results.corrected_locator: Methods 2.1 (weighting), 2.2.1 (violation definitions), 2.3 (cumulative estimation); Results 3.1 and 3.3; Tables 2 and 4, Total columns and Table 2 footnote 6/Table 4 footnote 3; Discussion 4.1

results.note: Section 2 specifies frequency of marijuana use in the population, i.e. population prevalence, rather than adjustment for an individual’s consumption frequency. It attributes the negligible-association assertion to Earleywine (2002). Section 3.2.1 and the captured references support the named biometrical genetic/twin citations. No discordant co-twin-control discussion was identified in the complete captured article body, and the intact L portion contains no Lynskey reference. Nevertheless, the file is explicitly truncated during V references, so I cannot certify the requested complete-reference-list check. Conclusions say the gateway hypothesis appears redundant, retaining a hedge. The Japan age-denominator mismatch is independently verified against the supplied Degenhardt text: 4.5%/4.8% are Table 2 ages 18-29, whereas 83.2% is Table 4 Total (18-29 value 77.3%). No systematic search or appraisal method is described in the captured article body.
results.corrected_extracted: The review asserts that the true cannabis–other-drug association is negligible when the frequency of cannabis use in the population is taken into account, attributing that assertion to Earleywine 2002 rather than presenting a new analysis of it. This refers to population prevalence, not control for individual consumption frequency. It cites biometrical genetic/twin and genetic-correlation studies, including Kendler 2003/2007 and Agrawal 2004. No discussion of discordant co-twin-control studies such as Lynskey 2003 was identified in the complete captured article body or available references; however, the supplied saved text is truncated partway through the V references and does not permit certification of the complete reference list. The Conclusions describe common liability as parsimonious and empirically proven and say that the gateway hypothesis appears redundant. No systematic search or appraisal is described. Its Japan example pairs the pooled age-at-interview Total estimate of 83.2% not-already-cannabis histories with cannabis and other-drug prevalences for 18–29-year-olds; these have different age denominators.

results.note: Visually confirmed across p.269 left-to-right columns and p.270 left-column continuation. The historical criteria are three or more substances excluding caffeine/nicotine, no dominant substance, and dependence for the group but not an individual substance. The review removes polysubstance dependence in DSM-5 and describes diagnosis by substance with severity grading. It does not name DSM-IV for this historical definition. The population-research frequency versus diagnostic criteria/severity statement appears on p.270. DSM-IV is mentioned elsewhere for a particular imaging study on p.272, which does not alter the narrower historical-definition claim.

Confirmed p.271 left column: national survey work includes simultaneous same-occasion use, and older groups reporting past-year polysubstance use are described as very likely also to report simultaneous use (ref.22). Here older is relative to the immediately discussed teen/young-adult context, not a defined elderly cohort. Both columns of p.272 support the mixed cognition summary: no behavioural differences in the discussed imaging, inhibition and decision-making comparisons; large differences on the five named standardized test domains outside the scanner (ref.62); and ref.51 associations between N-acetylaspartate and visuospatial/working-memory deficits. These are descriptions of cited studies, with no new pooled effect estimate or formal appraisal presented by this review.

The mixed findings and stronger concluding language are accurately located, but the review does not document how studies were selected or provide a design inventory establishing that they were unsystematically selected and largely cross-sectional. Absence of a reported systematic search is not proof of unsystematic selection. At least ref.55 is explicitly titled a prospective fMRI study on p.275. Retain the editorial caution while limiting the selection/design characterization to what this source establishes. The final p.272 paragraph says clearly associated with deficits, retaining an associational formulation; p.273 says the broader deficits place users at elevated risk of poorer treatment outcomes.
results.corrected_extracted: The review’s imaging section reports mixed cognitive findings, including null behavioural comparisons and large differences on standardized tests outside the scanner, then states that polysubstance abuse is clearly associated with deficits in brain function and cognition while acknowledging difficulties in specifying relationships because of methodological differences, the substances used and possibly limited statistical power. Its Conclusion states elevated psychiatric and health risk and more pervasive cognitive deficits that place users at elevated risk of poorer treatment outcomes, and judges prevention and treatment approaches underdeveloped. These broad conclusions warrant caution in light of the mixed findings summarized here (editorial appraisal). The review does not describe a systematic search or formal appraisal and does not supply a count of cross-sectional versus prospective designs; it should not be treated as proving unsystematic selection or a particular design distribution. This appraisal is not a claim that all cited cognitive results were null.

results.note: The Introduction starts the relevant evidential context on p.188 and makes the confounding/controls statements in the first left-column paragraph on p.189. It says overwhelming majority, difficult to draw conclusions, up to 234 polydrug ecstasy users and polydrug controls who did not use ecstasy, elevated psychopathology appeared associated with polydrug use generally, and controls mostly had more moderate drug use. The supplied wording is correct to leave unresolved whether 234 denotes the ecstasy group alone or the combined study sample. No inference from a separately retrieved primary study was made.

Both summary paragraphs on p.191 support some earlier investigations not capturing other-drug use, many poorly matched controls, possible pre-existing traits/general drug use/lifestyle, and the long-term prospective proposal. The eligibility wording is slightly broader and more conditional than the supplied extraction: the authors propose young people who are not or not yet users and who may belong to specific risk groups. They do not require every proposed participant to be established as at risk, nor do they unambiguously require every current non-user to be lifetime drug-naive. The replacement preserves this source hedge; all other material is supported.
results.corrected_extracted: The review says some earlier investigations did not capture parallel use of other drugs, and many studies used poorly matched controls. It does not characterize the missing other-drug data as occurring often. Findings may reflect pre-existing traits, drug use in general or associated lifestyle. The authors propose prospective work beginning with large cohorts of young people who are not or not yet users and may belong to specific risk groups, followed and re-examined over years with recorded drug histories and repeated tests of psychological functions and cognitive performance.
results.corrected_locator: Summary and perspectives for future research, first paragraph on missing other-drug data/control matching and second paragraph on prospective cohort proposal
